title: The Week the Stack Showed Its Age
excerpt: Microsoft went dark for a full day across 74 countries. Apple signed everyone out twice in one week. The FAA grounded every flight in America because a router from the 1980s failed. Nvidia lost its CEO to a spy scandal. And the banks started rewriting their terms to bar AI agents from touching accounts. One of these would be a headline. All of them happened in seven days.
description: Microsoft, Apple Pay, and the FAA all suffered major outages in one week while Nvidia lost its CEO and banks rewrote terms to block AI agents — a field report on what broke, why, and what it means for infrastructure trust.

twitterTitle: The week the stack showed its age
twitterDescription: Microsoft dark for 24 hours. Apple signed everyone out — twice. FAA grounded every flight because a 1980s router failed. Nvidia lost its CEO to a spy scandal. Banks are rewriting terms to block AI agents. All in seven days.
heroAlt: A cracked digital control panel with warning lights and old circuit boards behind a glowing modern city skyline at night
lede: Between November 11 and November 17, Microsoft went dark for 24 hours across 74 countries. Apple signed out every user and couldn't get them back in — twice in one week. The FAA grounded every domestic flight because a router replacement went wrong and the backup was a copper line from the 1980s. Nvidia's CEO resigned over an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, taking $1.76 trillion in market cap with him. And the four largest U.S. banks updated their terms of service to say AI agents cannot touch customer accounts. Any one of these is a news cycle. Together they are a stress test, and the stack failed it.

sections.heading: Microsoft: 24 hours, 74 countries, one network change
paras: Starting around 4:20 PM UTC on November 12, Outlook, Teams, and Copilot went offline across 74 countries. The outage lasted roughly 24 hours. Microsoft said the root cause was a network capacity upgrade from July that overloaded legacy gateway servers after a later configuration change. It was not a cyberattack. It was the third major Microsoft 365 outage of 2026.

House of Representatives staff told reporters the outage ended a day of legislative work. Enterprise customers across time zones lost email, calendar, file access, and the AI assistant Microsoft has spent the year pushing into every workflow. The pattern is familiar: a capacity change, a cascading fault, a system too tightly coupled to degrade gracefully. Eighteen hours is not a blip. It is a shift.

sections.heading: Apple: two outages in seven days
paras: On November 10, iCloud services including Mail, Calendar, Contacts, Photos, and Find My went down. Apple restored them. On November 17, an internal software update took out Apple Pay, iCloud, the App Store, Apple Music, and Apple sign-in. Users were signed out of their accounts. Some could not activate new iPhones. At peak, Downdetector logged 2,300 simultaneous reports.

Apple blamed the second outage on an internal update and said it was not a cyberattack. Services came back by evening. But two sign-in failures in one week means every person who relies on Apple Pay at a register, every developer whose app depends on Apple sign-in, and every business running on iCloud got a reminder that a single vendor's internal deployment can lock them out of their own money, identity, and data at the same time.

sections.heading: FAA: floppy disks, copper wire, and the second nationwide ground stop since 9/11
paras: On November 13 the FAA halted every domestic departure for approximately four hours — only the second nationwide ground stop since September 11, 2001. The cause was an equipment failure during a router replacement. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told Congress the system runs on 1980s-era screens, copper lines, and floppy disk drives. Some replacement parts are no longer manufactured.

More than 14,000 flights were cancelled between Friday and Saturday. Another 11,500 were disrupted on November 15. The GAO has found that 51 of 138 FAA systems are unsustainable, with another 54 potentially so, and that the agency spends more money sustaining legacy equipment than buying replacements. Duffy is asking Congress for $50 billion. In 2025, a single burned copper wire at Newark caused a 90-second communications blackout across the region.

Meanwhile, the FAA logged 601 drone sightings near U.S. airports in the second quarter of 2026 alone — nearly double the prior quarter. On June 29, a JetBlue pilot reported a possible drone collision on approach to JFK at 3,000 feet. On October 10, an American Airlines crew reported a near-miss after departing O'Hare. The airspace system cannot reliably identify, track, or respond to objects it was never designed to handle, and the hardware it runs on predates the internet.

sections.heading: Nvidia: the CEO, the spy, and $1.76 trillion
paras: On November 11, Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia effective immediately. The board accepted it the same day. Huang admitted to extramarital affairs; reporting has connected one of them to a woman allegedly linked to Chinese espionage. Nvidia hired Wachtell Lipton to investigate whether Huang's conduct compromised national security. The board said on its November 17 earnings call that it does not intend to reinstate him.

CFO Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO. The stock dropped more than four percent on the announcement, and reports estimate $1.76 trillion in market value was erased. Nvidia reported $115.8 billion in quarterly revenue on that same earnings call — a record — which means the company that dominates AI compute is posting its best numbers with a leadership vacuum at the top. Congress has summoned Huang to testify.

For the infrastructure story, the detail that matters is not the scandal. It is that a single person's departure destabilized the most valuable supply chain in AI. The chips, the CUDA stack, the data center roadmap — all of it ran through one executive's credibility, and that credibility evaporated in a news cycle.

sections.heading: The terms of service are moving faster than the technology
paras: While these outages were happening, the legal scaffolding around AI agents changed too. American Express, Bank of America, Citigroup, and JPMorgan Chase have all updated their terms of service to explicitly prohibit AI agents from using account credentials. Microsoft issued its third consecutive monthly rewrite of AI licensing terms. Google's July 30 update bars using AI output to build competing systems, and its advertising terms now make advertisers fully responsible for anything AI generates on their behalf.

Google's advertising terms now make advertisers fully responsible for anything AI generates on their behalf. X's 2026 terms give it a worldwide license to train on all user content, including AI-generated conversations, with no opt-out. A tracker monitoring 31 AI vendors found frequent small edits to terms between July and October 2026. The pattern is clear: companies are writing legal walls around their systems faster than anyone is building the technical interfaces to replace what those walls block. When a bank says an AI agent cannot log in with your credentials, it is not saying agents will not pay. It is saying agents will not pay through the existing stack. That is a gap, and it is growing.

sections.heading: What breaks when everything breaks at once
paras: Zoom out and the week draws one line through every story. Microsoft's outage is a coupling problem: one network change propagates because nothing in the architecture limits the blast radius. Apple's outage is a single-vendor problem: sign-in, payments, storage, and app distribution all fail together because they share one authentication layer. The FAA's outage is a legacy problem: the system works until it doesn't, and when it doesn't, there is no modern fallback. Nvidia's crisis is a concentration problem: the most important AI hardware company on earth had a single point of failure, and it was a person. The ToS rewrites are a boundary problem: the legal system is drawing lines the technical system has not built interfaces for yet.

Every one of these is a form of the same failure: a system that was built for one era running under the load of another. The load is AI-shaped. Agents that need to send payments, discover services, and settle transactions cannot wait 18 hours for Outlook to come back. They cannot authenticate through a system that signs everyone out twice a week. They cannot move money through terms of service that say they are not allowed to hold the credential.

The counter-pattern exists. It is small, it is early, and it is what we build on. An x402 payment settles in a block, not a batch. The agent holds its own credential — a wallet — so no vendor can sign it out. Discovery is a 402 response with a price, not an enterprise sales call. Settlement is on-chain and final, with no chargeback window and no terms-of-service clause that can revoke it after the fact. The architecture assumes the network will fail, the vendor will change its mind, and the agent will need to route around both.

sections.heading: The question for builders
paras: If you are building an agent that pays for things, the week of November 11 is a dataset. It tells you that the email layer can go dark for a business day. It tells you that the payment layer can lock out every user because of an internal deployment. It tells you that the physical infrastructure underneath all of it is running on hardware older than the developers maintaining it. And it tells you that the legal teams at the largest financial institutions in the world are actively closing the door on agents using traditional payment rails.

None of this means those systems are going away. It means they are showing where they bend, and the bends are getting deeper. The question is not whether to build on something more resilient. The question is how long you wait.
